A system of linear equations is of the form    a11x1 + a12x2 + · · · + a1nxn = b1 a21x1 + a22x2 + · · · + a2nxn = b2 ... am1x1 + am2x2 + · · · + amnxn = bm ⇐⇒ x1      a11 a21 ... am1      + · · · + xn      a1n a2n ... amn      =      b1 b2 ... bm      . In matrix notation, the equation above is written as Ax = b where A ∈ Mm×n(F ), x ∈ F n and b ∈ F m. If b = 0, then the system is called homogeneous. If b ̸= 0, the system is called inhomogeneous. We identify the system with the matrix A so we will refer to some columns as variables and variables as columns. Definition 7.2. A matrix is in row reduced echelon form (RREF) if (i) All zero rows, if any, are at the bottom. (ii) In each nonzero row, the first nonzero entry (called a pivot) appears to the right of the pivot in the row above. (iii) Each pivot equals 1. (iv) Each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column. The non-pivot columns are called free variables. Theorem 7.3. For every matrix A ∈ Mm×n(F ), one can apply elementary row opera- tions to reduce A to a matrix R in RREF. (i) The number of pivot columns in R is rank A. The columns of the original matrix A corresponding to the pivot columns form a basis for im A. (ii) The number of free variables is n − rank A = null A. To find a basis for ker A, assign 1 to one free variable and 0 to the others, then solve the resulting system for the pivot variables, repeat this for each free variable. The resulting vectors form a basis for ker A. (iii) The nonzero rows of R form a basis for im At. (iv) The RREF of a matrix A is unique. Remark 7.4. The pivot column must be a basis of im A but a basis of im A does not have to be the pivot columns. Definition 7.5. The augmented matrix [A | b] is the matrix obtained by appending the column vector b ∈ F m on the right to a matrix A ∈ Mm×n(F ). Theorem 7.6. The system Ax = b has a solution if and only if the last column in the RREF of [A | b] is not a pivot column. If Ax = b has a solution, then solutions of Ax = b is given by solving the pivot variables in terms of the free variables. 36 We recall that Theorem 6.15 (ii) says im A = (ker At)⊥. This is a dual space criterion which we can test solvability of Ax = b. Theorem 7.7. The equation Ax = b has a solution if and only if for any y ∈ F m such that Aty = 0 we have ytb = 0. Proof. (iv) Suppose R and R′ are two RREF of A. Then R′ = P ′A and R = P A where P and P ′ are products of elementary matrices. Then R′ = QR and where Q = P ′P −1 39 is invertible. As above, we assume R = (Ir C 0 0 ) where C = (cij) ∈ Mr×(n−r)(F ). We write Q = (Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 ) where Q1 ∈ Mr×r(F ), Q2 ∈ Mr×(n−r)(F ), Q3 ∈ M(n−r)×r and Q4 ∈ M(n−r)×(n−r)(F ). Then R′ = QR = ( Q1 Q1C Q3 Q3C ). By (i), the number of pivots is rank A = r. Thus by definition of RREF, the last m − r rows of R′ are 0. Hence Q3 = 0. We claim that Q1 is invertible. Indeed, if this is not the case, then the first r columns of Q = (Q1 Q2 0 Q4 ) are linearly dependent. This contradicts the fact that Q is invertible. Thus Q1 is invertible. Since R′ = (Q1 Q1C 0 0 ) is in RREF and the first r columns are linearly independent, they must all be the pivot columns since any non-pivot column is a linear combination of the pivot columns to the left of it. Thus using the definition of RREF, Q1 = Ir. Hence R′ = R. Corollary 7.9. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) be invertible. Then there exists elementary matrices E1, . . . , Em such that A = E1 · · · Em. Proof. Since A is invertible, rank A = n. Then by Theorem 7.3, every column of A is a pivot column. Since pivot column in an RREF consist of 1 at the pivot and 0 elsewhere, the RREF for A is I. Since the Gauss Elmination is multiplying elementary matrices M1, . . . , Mm to the left of A, we have Mm · · · M1A = I and hence A = E1 · · · Em where Ei = M −1 i is also an elementary matrix. Corollary 7.10. Compute A−1 using Gauss elimination: 1. Start with the augmented matrix [A | I] 2. Perform row operations to reduce the left side A to the identity matrix. 3. The result will be [I | A−1] where the right block becomes the inverse of A. Computationally, row operations correspond to multiplying by elementary matrices, so the whole process is: Ek · · · E2E1A = I =⇒ A−1 = Ek · · · E2E1. If at any step we cannot reduce A to the identity (e.g., a pivot is zero and cannot be fixed by swapping rows), then A is not invertible. Proof of Theorem 7.6. If the last column of [A | b] is a pivot, then the last nonzero rows of the RREF of [A | b] contains a row of the form (0 0 · · · 0 | 1). This corresponds to the equation 0x1 + 0x2 + · · · + 0xn = 1 which has no solution. If the last column in the RREF of [A | b] is not a pivot column, then the pivot appears in columns of A. Hence a basis of im[A | b] is a basis of im A i.e. im[A | b] = im A. Hence b = Ax for some x ∈ F n. To find all solutions to Ax = b we write the RREF of [A | b] as ( Ir (cij) ˜b 0 0 0 ) after permuting columns. Remark 7.11. What if b /∈ im A but we want to find the x such that Ax is closest to b? You would need the least square method which is covered in Linear Algebra II. 7.2 Determinant Let v1, . . . , v3 ∈ R3. We write vol(v1, v2, v3) to be the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by v1, v2, v3. The signed volume of v1, v2, v3, denoted by det(v1, v2, v3) is a function that gives vol(v1, v2, v3) if v1, v2, v3 are right handed and −vol(v1, v2, v3) if v1, v2, v3 are left handed. The determinant is the n-dimensional generalization of this which satisfies the properties in the following definition. Definition 7.12. The determinant is a function det : Mn×n(F ) → F satisfying the following properties. We write A = (v1 . . . vn) where vi ∈ F n are the columns of A. (i) det is multilinear in columns: If for some 1 ≤ j ≤ n, vj = ax + by where a, b ∈ F x, y ∈ F n, then det(v1, . . . , ax + by, . . . , vn) = a det(v1, . . . , x, . . . , vn) + b det(v1, . . . , y, . . . , vn). (ii) det alternative in column: If vi = vj for i ̸= j, then det(v1 . . . vn) = 0. (iii) det I = 1. Lemma 7.13. Suppose det : Mn×n(F ) → F is a function satisfying (i), (ii), (iii) of Definition 7.12. Then we have the following (i) det(v1 . . . 0 . . . vn) = 0. (ii) det(. . . vi . . . vj . . . ) = − det(. . . vj . . . vi . . . ). (iii) det(v1 . . . vj + ∑ i̸=j λivi . . . vn) = det(v1 . . . vj . . . vn) Proof. (i) By multilinearity, det(v1 . . . 0 . . . vn) = 0 det(v1 . . . 0 . . . vn) = 0. 41 (ii) det(. . . , vi . . . vj, . . . ) + det(. . . , vj . . . vi, . . . ) = det(. . . , vi . . . vj, . . . ) + det(. . . , vi . . . vi, . . . ) + det(. . . , vj . . . vj, . . . ) + det(. . . , vj . . . vi, . . . ) = det(. . . , vi . . . vi + vj, . . . ) + det(. . . , vj . . . vi + vj, . . . ) = det(. . . , vi + vj . . . vi + vj, . . . ) =0. (iii) By multilinearity in the j-th column, we can expand: det(v1 . . . vj + ∑ i̸=j λivi . . . vn) = det(v1 . . . vj . . . vn) + ∑ i̸=j λi det(v1 . . . vi . . . vn), where in each term of the sum, the j-th column has been replaced by vi. By the alternating property, each determinant in the sum vanishes, since two columns are equal in each: det(. . . , vi . . . vi, . . . ) = 0. Therefore, det(v1 . . . vj + ∑ i̸=j λivi . . . vn) = det(v1 . . . vj . . . vn) 42
